subject: History
source: National Curriculum KS1 (changes within living memory); no school Drive history material found for Y1, written from scratch

lessons.title: Past, present and future
objectives: Use the words past, present and future correctly
Sort things into old and new

keywords.def: things that have not happened yet
made or used a long time ago

starter: What did you eat for breakfast today?
What do you think you will do tomorrow?

teach.heading: Bismillah: what is history?
bullets: History is the story of the past
The past is what has already happened
Today we learn to be history detectives
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Ask: has anyone been a detective before? Explain that historians look for clues to find out what life was like long ago.

teach.heading: Past, present, future
teach.note: Hold up three cards (yesterday, today, tomorrow). Pupils point to the right card as you say a sentence, e.g. 'I ate my lunch an hour ago'. Misconception: 'the past' only means a very long time ago; an hour ago is also the past.

teach.heading: Old and new objects
bullets: A telephone with a cord is old
Old things can show us the past
teach.note: Show two pictures: a landline telephone with a curly cord and a mobile phone. Ask which one grandparents used when they were children. Praise the words 'old' and 'new'.

teach.heading: Words that help us
bullets: Long ago, a long time ago
teach.note: Practise the vocabulary with actions: pupils point behind them for 'past', in front for 'future', down for 'now'.

practice: Teacher says: 'We ate breakfast.' Is that past, present or future?
Teacher says: 'We are on Teams now.' Is that past, present or future?
Teacher says: 'We will go to bed tonight.' Is that past, present or future?
independent: Draw one thing you did yesterday, one thing you are doing now and one thing you will do tomorrow
Label your three drawings past, present and future
Say one sentence about your picture using the word 'yesterday'
exit: Is yesterday the past, present or future?
Is a mobile phone old or new?
lessons.homework: Ask a grown-up at home to show you one old object and one new object, and tell the class about them next lesson.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use picture cards and gestures for past, present, future and accept pointing as an answer. Stretch: add the words 'last week' and 'next week' to the sorting.

lessons.title: My own timeline
objectives: Put events from my own life in order
Use words such as baby, toddler and now

keywords.def: a line that puts events in the order they happened
which comes first, next and last
how many years old you are

starter: Is yesterday in the past or the future?
Name one old object and one new object.
What word do we use for what is happening now?

teach.heading: Changes in me
teach.note: Say bismillah and thank Allah for how we grow. Show three pictures of a child as a baby, a toddler and a school child (a drawing is fine). Ask what changed.

teach.heading: What is a timeline?
bullets: A timeline shows events in order
The earliest event goes on the left
teach.note: Model a timeline on screen using a strip of paper: Baby, Toddler, Reception, Year 1. Point left to right as you read.

teach.heading: Using age as a clue
teach.note: Link ages to events. Ask pupils: what could you not do as a baby but can do now? Collect answers such as walk, read, write.

teach.heading: Photographs are clues
bullets: Old photos show how we looked
They help us find out about the past
teach.note: Show a baby photo and a recent photo. Ask what clues tell us which is older. Misconception: the photo that is bigger or colourful is older; look at the child's size.

practice: Order these: Year 1, baby, toddler. Which comes first?
What could you do when you were a baby? What can you do now?
Point to where 'now' goes on our class timeline
independent: Draw yourself as a baby, as a toddler and now on a three-box timeline
Write the words first, next, now under the boxes
Tell your partner one new thing you can do now
exit: Which comes first on your timeline: baby or Year 1?
Say one thing you can do now that you could not do as a baby.
lessons.homework: Find one baby photo or baby item at home and bring it (or describe it) to show your teacher.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a pre-drawn three-box timeline with pictures to cut and stick or drag. Stretch: add a fourth box for 'when I am grown up' and label it future.

lessons.title: Toys from long ago and toys today
objectives: Say how toys today are different from toys in the past
Use the words old and new to compare toys

keywords.def: a light material made in factories
to say how things are the same and different

starter: Which comes first: baby or Year 1?
Say a sentence using the word 'yesterday'.

teach.heading: Toys long ago
bullets: Many old toys were made of wood or metal
teach.note: Show pictures of a wooden spinning top, a wooden doll or a tin toy, and a hoop and stick. Say that these toys were used by children many years ago, before our grandparents were born in some cases.

teach.heading: Toys today
bullets: Many toys today are made of plastic
Some toys use batteries or screens
Toys are made in big factories
teach.note: Show a plastic building brick set and a battery toy. Ask: which materials can you see? Introduce the word 'material'.

teach.heading: Same and different
bullets: Same: children play and have fun
Different: materials and how they work
Different: old toys often have no batteries
teach.note: Make a two-column chart 'old toy' and 'new toy' live on screen. Accept simple answers. Misconception: children long ago had no toys; they did, but different ones.

teach.heading: Looking after toys
teach.note: Link to adab: in Islam we are taught to be kind, to share and not to waste. Keep this brief and positive.

practice: Is a wooden spinning top an old toy or a new toy?
Name one material a toy can be made of.
Say one way an old toy is different from a toy today.
independent: Draw one old toy and one new toy
Write old and new under your pictures
Say one sentence: 'The old toy is made of ... The new toy is made of ...'
exit: Name one thing that is the same about old toys and new toys.
Name one thing that is different.
lessons.homework: Choose your favourite toy at home. Find out what it is made of and tell your teacher.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide sentence frames 'The old toy is ...' with a word bank (wood, plastic, metal). Stretch: sort toys into wood, plastic and metal.

lessons.title: Asking questions about the past
objectives: Ask a question to find out about the past
Understand that people can tell us about the past

keywords.def: something we ask to find out an answer
the mother or father of your parent
to keep something in your mind from the past
clues that help us find out

starter: What is a toy made of?

teach.heading: History detectives
bullets: Clues can be objects, photos or people
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Remind pupils of the detective idea from lesson 1. Explain that the best clue is sometimes a person who was there.

teach.heading: Asking good questions
teach.note: Model question words What, Who, Where. Show how a question starts with a capital letter and ends with a question mark. Ask pupils to make up their own.

teach.heading: Listening to answers
teach.note: Role-play with a pretend grandparent (you). Answer in simple terms, e.g. 'I played with marbles and a skipping rope.' Show respect to elders as part of adab.

teach.heading: What we found out
bullets: Old people remember games from long ago
Some old games need no toys
Some games are still played today
teach.note: Mention skipping, hopscotch and marbles as games still played. Ask: why do you think they are still popular?

practice: Choose a question word to start: ___ did you play with?
Who could you ask to find out about toys long ago?
Practise asking your partner: What is your favourite game?
independent: Write or draw one question to ask a grandparent or older person about their toys
Draw the answer you think they will give
Say your question out loud to the class
exit: Who can tell us about the past?
Say one question you could ask about toys long ago.
lessons.homework: Ask an older person at home your question about toys and bring back one answer.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a question starter strip (What / Who / Where) and allow drawing. Stretch: ask a second follow-up question beginning with Why.
